Landlocked country in the [[Horn of Africa]], East Africa (pop., 2026: around 138 million). Officially the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, it covers a land area of 1,104,300 km² and is the 10th-most populous country in the world and the 2nd most populous in Africa. The capital and largest city, [[Addis Ababa]], lies several kilometers west of the East African Rift, which splits the country into the African and Somali tectonic plates.

Anatomically modern humans emerged in what is now Ethiopia. The [[Kingdom of Aksum]] maintained a unified civilization in the region for 900 years, and Christianity arrived there in 330 AD. Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty in 1270, inaugurating the [[Ethiopian Empire]] and the Solomonic dynasty, which asserted descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Under [[Menelik II]], the empire expanded, remained independent during the Scramble for Africa, and defeated an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa in 1896. Italy invaded again in the [[Second Italo-Ethiopian War]], and Ethiopia lost its sovereignty in 1936; British forces liberated it in 1941, and full sovereignty was restored in 1944. The [[Derg]], a Soviet-backed military junta, took power in 1974 after deposing Emperor Haile Selassie and ruled for nearly 17 years. After 1991 the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front dominated the country under a new constitution establishing ethnic-based federalism. Since 2018, regional and ethnically based factions have carried out armed attacks in multiple ongoing wars.

Ethiopia has more than 80 ethnic groups. Christianity is the most widely professed faith, the largest denomination being the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, followed by Islam. The country is a founding member of the UN, hosts the headquarters of the [[African Union]] Commission, and became a full member of BRICS in 2024. Agriculture is the largest economic sector, accounting for over 37% of GDP as of 2022. Despite consistent growth, Ethiopia remains among the poorest countries in Africa in per capita income, with a literacy rate of 60%.

Group of people who identify with one another on the basis of perceived shared attributes that distinguish them from other groups. The attributes may include language, culture, common ancestry, traditions, society, religion, history, region, or social treatment. Ethnic identities may rest on a narrow or broad spectrum of genetic ancestry, and some groups have mixed ancestry. Ethnicity is sometimes used interchangeably with [[Nation|nation]], and also with [[Race (human categorization)|race]], although not all ethnicities identify as racial groups.

Individuals or groups may shift from one ethnic group to another over time through assimilation, acculturation, amalgamation, language shift, intermarriage, adoption, and religious conversion. Ethnic groups may divide into subgroups or tribes, which can become separate ethnic groups in turn through endogamy or physical isolation. Formerly separate ethnicities may also merge into a panethnicity. The formation of a separate ethnic identity, whether through division or amalgamation, is called ethnogenesis, a term in use in ethnological literature since about 1950.

The word *ethnic* derives from the Greek *ethnos*, through the adjective *ethnikos*, borrowed into Latin as *ethnicus*. In Early Modern English and until the mid-19th century it meant "heathen" or "pagan," because the [[Septuagint]] used *ta ethne*, "the nations," to translate the Hebrew *goyim*. The sense of "different cultural groups" arose in the 1930s and 1940s, replacing *race*, which was becoming deprecated because of its association with ideological racism. *Ethnic group* was first recorded in 1935 and entered the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] in 1972. *Nationality* may mean either ethnicity or [[Citizenship|citizenship]], depending on context.

Groups can be classified by the source of identity emphasized: ethno-linguistic (French Canadians), ethno-national (Austrians), ethno-racial (African Americans), ethno-regional (South Islanders of New Zealand), ethno-religious (Sikhs, [[Jews]]), ethno-civic (ancient Romans), and ethno-cultural (Travellers). These categories often overlap, and membership is frequently determined by more than one aspect. Armenian ethnicity, for example, can be defined by citizenship, heritage, native use of the Armenian language, or membership of the Armenian Apostolic Church.

Ethnography begins in classical antiquity, and [[Herodotus]] laid the foundation of both historiography and ethnography of the ancient world c. 480 BC. He gave a famous account of Greek identity as shared descent, shared language, shared sanctuaries and sacrifices, and shared customs. The orator Isocrates, by contrast, wrote that the name Hellenes applied to those who shared Athenian culture rather than a common blood.

Two main theories exist in understanding ethnicities, primordialism and constructivism. Early 20th-century primordialists viewed ethnic groups as real phenomena whose distinct characteristics have endured since the distant past. Perspectives that developed after the 1960s increasingly viewed ethnic groups as social constructs, with identity assigned by societal rules. Thomas Hylland Eriksen describes a debate between primordialism, in which ethnic ties are seen as an externally given social bond, and instrumentalism, which treats ethnicity as an element of political strategy used to gain wealth, power, or status. Anthropologists such as Fredrik Barth and Eric Wolf do not consider ethnic identity universal, regarding it as a product of specific kinds of inter-group interactions. Other accounts emphasize that ethnic affiliations often correspond to patterns of genetic similarity formed through endogamy and relative isolation, and they dispute the view that ethnicity is purely a social invention.

Ancient Greek mathematician (fl. 300 BC), active as a geometer and logician in [[Alexandria]]. Considered the "father of geometry," he is chiefly known for the *Elements*, a 13-book treatise that established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. The [[Euclid's Elements|*Elements*]] deduces theorems from a small set of axioms, beginning with definitions, postulates, and common notions. Its system, now called [[Euclidean geometry]], combined innovations with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales, and Theaetetus. With [[Archimedes]] and [[Apollonius of Perga]], Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity.

Very little is known of his life, and most information comes from the scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria, writing many centuries later. Proclus placed him during the rule of Ptolemy I (r. 305/304–282 BC), after the followers of [[Plato]] and before Archimedes. His birthplace is unknown. It is often presumed that he was educated by Plato's disciples at the Platonic Academy in Athens, though one historian considers this mere conjecture. Pappus mentions that Apollonius studied with Euclid's students in Alexandria, which has been taken to imply that Euclid worked and founded a mathematical tradition there, possibly among the first scholars of the Musaeum.

Euclid is often called "Euclid of Alexandria" to distinguish him from Euclid of Megara, a pupil of [[Socrates]]. Medieval Byzantine sources conflated the two, and printed editions of the *Elements*, including one in 1482 and a translation by Bartolomeo Zamberti in 1505, passed the confusion on. Renaissance scholars later disproved it on chronological grounds.

Besides the *Elements*, he is accepted as the author of three other mostly extant treatises: *Optics*, an early text in the field of [[Optics|optics]], *Data*, and *Phaenomena*. He also wrote on perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, number theory, and mathematical rigor, and his authorship of *On Divisions of Figures* and *Catoptrics* has been questioned. He is thought to have written many lost works. Questions about the fifth postulate, concerning parallel lines, later led mathematicians to non-Euclidean geometries, among them the work of Nikolai Lobachevsky in 1829.

Organism of the domain Eukaryota (or Eukarya), whose cells have a distinct [[Cell nucleus|nucleus]] enclosed by a nuclear membrane, membrane-bound organelles, and organization supported by a [[Cytoskeleton|cytoskeleton]]. Extant eukaryotes are traditionally grouped into four kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi, and [[Protist|protists]]. Protists are a basal paraphyletic group that includes all algae, amoebae, flagellates, and ciliates. In the prevailing three-domain system, eukaryotes stand alongside the two domains of [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]], Bacteria and Archaea. Cladistically, however, eukaryotes emerged within the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota, which would imply only two domains of life.

Eukaryotes first emerged during the Paleoproterozoic. The leading evolutionary theory holds that they resulted from a [[Symbiogenesis|symbiogenesis]] between an anaerobic archaeon and an aerobic alphaproteobacterium that became the proto-[[Mitochondria|mitochondrion]], in response to the oxidative stress following the Great Oxygenation Event. A second symbiogenetic event during the Mesoproterozoic, between a protist host and a cyanobacterial endosymbiont, produced the [[Chloroplast|chloroplast]] and the photosynthetic clade Archaeplastida, which includes green algae, red algae, glaucophytes, and land plants.

Eukaryotic cells are typically much larger than prokaryotic ones. Their organelles include the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, ribosomes, vacuoles, and lysosomes, as well as endosymbiont-derived organelles bound by two or more membrane layers, such as mitochondria and plastids. Genetic information is divided among multiple linear DNA molecules called chromosomes, packaged by histone proteins and held inside the nucleus. Eukaryotes reproduce asexually through [[Mitosis|mitosis]] and sexually through meiosis and gamete fusion. Their larger size and more complex architecture allow phagocytosis, which enables microscopic predation of other unicellular organisms.

Eukaryotes range from picozoans under 3 micrometers across to the blue whale, weighing up to 190 tonnes and measuring up to 33.6 m, and the coast redwood, up to 120 m tall. Many are unicellular. Multicellularity has evolved independently at least 25 times within the group, and complex multicellular organisms have evolved in only six lineages: animals, symbiomycotan fungi, brown algae, red algae, green algae, and land plants. Eukaryotes are a small minority of organisms by number, but their collective biomass of 468 gigatons far exceeds that of prokaryotes at 77 gigatons, with plants alone accounting for over 81% of the total biomass of Earth.

Continent lying entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and mostly in the Eastern Hemisphere, forming the western part of Eurasia. It is bordered by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, the Mediterranean Sea to the south, and Asia to the east. Europe is commonly considered to be separated from Asia by the watershed of the [[Ural Mountains]], the Ural River, the Caspian Sea, the Greater Caucasus, the Black Sea, and the Turkish straits. Islands are generally grouped with the nearest continental landmass, so Iceland is part of Europe while Greenland is usually assigned to North America. Cyprus, though closest to Anatolia, is considered European politically.

Europe covers approximately 10,186,000 sq km, or 2% of Earth's surface (6.8% of its land area), making it the second-smallest continent in the seven-continent model. It is politically divided into about fifty sovereign states, of which Russia is the largest and most populous, spanning 39% of the continent and comprising 15% of its population. Europe had a total population of about 745 million, about 10% of the world population, in 2021, the third-largest after Asia and Africa. Warm Atlantic currents such as the [[Gulf Stream]] produce a temperate climate across much of the continent, while regions farther from the sea have more continental climates.

The name derives from Europa, a Phoenician princess of Greek mythology. One view derives it from Greek elements meaning "wide" and "eye" or "face"; Robert Beekes argued for a pre-Indo-European origin, and a proposed link to a Semitic word for "west" has been judged improbable by scholars. Most major world languages use words derived from it.

European culture consists of national and regional cultures that form central roots of Western civilization and commonly reference ancient Greece and ancient Rome, particularly through their Christian successors. The fall of the [[Western Roman Empire]] in 476 CE and the Christian consolidation that followed the Migration Period marked the Middle Ages. The Italian [[Renaissance]] spread across many Western European countries, and its renewed humanist emphasis on art and science contributed to the transition to the modern era. Since the [[Age of Discovery]], led by Spain and Portugal, Europe played a predominant role in global affairs. Between the 16th and 20th centuries, European powers colonized the Americas, almost all of Africa and Oceania, and the majority of Asia. The Age of Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and the Napoleonic Wars shaped the continent from the end of the 17th century until the first half of the 19th century. The [[Industrial Revolution]], which began in Great Britain at the end of the 18th century, brought radical economic, cultural, and social change.

Both world wars began and were fought largely in Europe, contributing to a decline in Western European dominance by the mid-20th century as the Soviet Union and the United States took prominence. The [[Cold War]] divided the continent along the Iron Curtain, with NATO in the West and the Warsaw Pact in the East. The divide ended with the Revolutions of 1989, the fall of the Berlin Wall, and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, which allowed European integration to advance. Integration has proceeded institutionally since the founding of the Council of Europe in 1949, and above all through the [[European Union]], which represents the majority of the continent. A majority of its members use the euro, and a large bloc of countries in the Schengen Area has abolished internal border controls.

Supranational political and economic union of 27 member states located primarily in Europe. It has a total area of 4,233,255 km² and an estimated population of just under 452 million as of 2026. Its member states generated a nominal gross domestic product of around €18.802 trillion in 2025, approximately one sixth of global economic output. The EU is often described as a *sui generis* entity combining characteristics of a federation and a confederation.

Its cornerstone, the Customs Union, paved the way for an internal single market based on a standardized legal framework that applies in all member states only in those matters where the states have agreed to act as one. EU policies aim to ensure the free movement of people, goods, services, and capital; enact legislation in justice and home affairs; and maintain common policies on trade, agriculture, fisheries, and regional development. Passport controls have been abolished for travel within the [[Schengen Area]]. The eurozone comprises the 21 member states that use the [[Euro|euro]]. Through the Common Foreign and Security Policy, the union has developed a role in external relations and defense, maintains diplomatic missions throughout the world, and represents itself at the [[United Nations]], the [[World Trade Organization]], the G7, and the G20. It was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012.

Internationalism and visions of European unity gained force as a reaction to World War I and its aftermath. [[Winston Churchill]], speaking at the University of Zürich in 1946, reiterated his calls for a "European Union" and a "Council of Europe." The Union's beginnings can be traced to the Inner Six states (Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and West Germany) at the start of modern [[European integration]] in 1948, and to bodies including the European Coal and Steel Community, the European Economic Community, and the European Atomic Energy Community, established by treaties. The EU was established, along with its citizenship, when the Maastricht Treaty came into force in 1993, and it acquired a single international legal personality with the Treaty of Lisbon in 2009. A further 22 states joined from 1973 to 2013. In 2020 the [[United Kingdom]] became the only member state to leave, and ten countries are aspiring or negotiating to join. Critics cite a democratic deficit, including the appointed European Commission's monopoly on legislative initiative, while supporters credit the Union with decades of peace among former rivals.

Large-scale colonization of North, Central, and South America by European powers, primarily between the late 15th century and early 19th century, during the [[Age of Discovery]]. The Norse had settled areas of the North Atlantic earlier, colonizing Greenland and creating a short-lived settlement near the northern tip of Newfoundland c. 1000 AD. The remains of that settlement, L'Anse aux Meadows, were discovered in 1960 and are the only site widely accepted as evidence of pre-Columbian trans-oceanic contact.

Systematic, long-term colonization began in 1492, when a Spanish expedition led by [[Christopher Columbus]], seeking a new trade route to the Orient, landed in The Bahamas. Ottoman control of trade routes to Asia had pushed European monarchs to seek alternatives. Under the [[Treaty of Tordesillas]] of 1494, Portugal and Spain agreed to divide the world between them; Spanish claims covered essentially all the Americas, while Portugal received the eastern tip of South America, where it established Brazil in the early 1500s. [[Santo Domingo]], founded in 1496, is credited as the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the Americas.

By the 1530s other Western European powers had begun to participate. The British and French colonized the northeastern part of the continent, with [[Jamestown]] founded in 1607 and [[Quebec]] in 1608. The Dutch founded New Amsterdam in 1624, the Swedes established New Sweden, and Denmark–Norway, Sweden, and the Netherlands colonized parts of the Caribbean. By the 1700s Russia had begun to explore and claim the Pacific Coast from Alaska to California. Many religions, political boundaries, and lingua francas that predominate in the Western Hemisphere today descend from structures established in this period.

The [[Columbian exchange]] transferred crops, livestock, and technologies between hemispheres, and introduced pathogens such as smallpox, measles, and influenza to Indigenous populations without prior exposure. Indigenous peoples suffered epidemic disease, displacement, and enslavement, and some accounts characterize the violence as genocide; accounts differ over the relative weight of violence and disease in the decline of Indigenous populations. Indigenous peoples also fought to preserve their territorial integrity, and conflict between European empires and Indigenous nations remained a leading dynamic into the 1800s. The United States pursued a settler colonial policy of [[Manifest destiny]] and Indian removal. Some regions, including California, Patagonia, and the northern Great Plains, experienced little or no colonization until the 1800s. By the 19th century, independence movements had reshaped much of the Americas into nation-states.

Change in the heritable characteristics of biological populations over successive generations. It occurs when individuals in a population vary in their genetic characteristics and in the numbers of their surviving offspring. [[Mutation]] introduces new genetic variation, and processes such as [[Genetic drift|genetic drift]], gene flow, and natural selection make some variants more or less common over time. Evolution is often defined as a change in the frequency of alleles, the variants of a gene found at a specific locus, in a population. In a strict biological sense it can occur even when the visible phenotype is unchanged, because alleles do not necessarily have a visible effect. The process has given rise to biodiversity at every level of biological organization.

The scientific theory of evolution by [[Natural selection|natural selection]] was conceived independently by two British naturalists, [[Charles Darwin]] and [[Alfred Russel Wallace]], in the mid-19th century, as an explanation for why organisms are adapted to their environments. Their ideas were jointly presented in 1858, and the theory was first set out in detail in Darwin's 1859 book [[On the Origin of Species|*On the Origin of Species*]]. Natural selection rests on four observable facts: more offspring are often produced than can survive; traits vary among individuals; different traits confer different rates of survival and reproduction; and traits can be passed from generation to generation. Members of a population are therefore more likely to be replaced by the offspring of parents with favorable characteristics for that environment.

In the early 20th century, competing ideas of evolution were refuted and evolution was combined with [[Mendelian inheritance]] and population genetics to give rise to modern evolutionary theory. In this synthesis, the basis of heredity is in DNA molecules that pass information from generation to generation. DNA is a long polymer composed of four types of bases, and portions that specify a single functional unit are called genes. Each long strand of DNA is a chromosome, the location of a sequence within it is a locus, and the different forms of a sequence at a locus are alleles. The complete set of genes in an organism is its genotype, and the set of observable traits is its phenotype. Some observable characteristics are not inherited; a suntan, for example, results from the interaction of genotype and sunlight and is not passed to children.

Variation comes from mutations in the genome, reshuffling of genes through sexual reproduction, and migration between populations. Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence and are the ultimate source of genetic variation. About half of the mutations in the coding regions of protein-coding genes are deleterious and the other half neutral, with a small percentage conferring a benefit. Duplication of large sections of a chromosome introduces extra copies of genes, a major source of raw material for new genes. A new allele may eventually reach fixation, when it either disappears from the population or replaces the ancestral allele entirely.

All life on Earth shares a [[Last universal common ancestor|last universal common ancestor]], which lived approximately 3.5–3.8 billion years ago. The fossil record includes a progression from early biogenic graphite to microbial mat fossils to fossilized multicellular organisms. Existing biodiversity has been shaped by repeated formation of new species, changes within species, and extinction. Species that share a more recent common ancestor tend to be more similar in morphological and biochemical traits, which was historically used to reconstruct phylogenetic trees, although direct comparison of genetic sequences is now more common. Evolutionary discoveries have influenced agriculture, medicine, and computer science. Supporting evidence includes fossil records documenting transitional forms, comparative genomics revealing shared ancestry, and observable changes in real time, such as antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

Physical activity that enhances or maintains fitness and overall health. It is performed for many reasons, including weight loss or maintenance, building strength, developing [[Muscle|muscles]] and the cardiovascular system, honing athletic skills, improving health, or simple enjoyment. Many people exercise outdoors, where they can socialize and improve well-being and [[Mental health|mental health]]. Exercise is a subset of physical activity: it is planned, structured, and repetitive, and aims to improve or maintain components of [[Physical fitness|physical fitness]].

Exercises are generally grouped into three types. Aerobic exercise uses large muscle groups and causes the body to use more oxygen than at rest, with the goal of increasing cardiovascular endurance; examples are running, cycling, swimming, and brisk walking. Anaerobic exercise, which includes strength and resistance training, can strengthen and increase muscle mass and improve bone density, balance, and coordination; examples are push-ups, squats, and sprinting. Flexibility exercises, such as stretching, improve joint flexibility and range of motion, which can reduce the chance of injury. Exercise may also be classified as dynamic or static: steady running tends to lower diastolic blood pressure during exercise, whereas weight-lifting can raise systolic pressure significantly but transiently.

Regular exercise contributes to a healthy weight, healthy bone density, muscle strength, and joint mobility, reduces surgical risks, and strengthens the immune system. People who exercise at moderate to high levels have a lower mortality rate than those who are physically inactive. Low levels of exercise raise the risk of [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]] and are an independent risk factor for [[Coronary artery disease|coronary artery disease]]. Physical inactivity causes approximately 6% of the burden of disease from coronary heart disease, 7% of type 2 diabetes, 10% of breast cancer, and 10% of colon cancer worldwide, and 9% of premature mortality overall. Most benefits are achieved at around 3500 metabolic equivalent (MET) minutes per week, with diminishing returns at higher levels, and even half the usual recommended amount reduces the risk of early death, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and [[Cancer|cancer]].

Recommendations vary by source. One commonly cited figure is 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week. The World Health Organization recommends that adults do at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity per week, with muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days, and that children and adolescents do at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily. Even a small amount is healthier than none: for people who get the least activity, adding two or three minutes per day of moderate activity could reduce the risk of premature death by 10%.

Reactive substance containing a great amount of potential energy that can produce an explosion if released suddenly, usually accompanied by light, heat, sound, and pressure. An explosive may be a single ingredient or a mixture, and can be combined with mechanical or electronic components to make a bomb. The energy is most commonly stored chemically, as in [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]], [[TNT]], or [[Nitroglycerin|nitroglycerin]], less commonly as pressurized gas, or as nuclear energy in fissile isotopes such as [[Uranium-235|uranium-235]].

Explosives are categorized by reaction speed. High explosives detonate, with the reaction front moving through the material faster than the speed of sound; low explosives deflagrate, with the front moving slower, producing a rapid burn rather than a proper explosion. By sensitivity, primary explosives can be initiated by a small amount of heat or pressure, while secondary and tertiary explosives are relatively insensitive and need a detonator. Only some manufactured chemicals are suitable, since others are too dangerous, sensitive, toxic, expensive, or unstable. Dusts, powders, gases, and volatile liquids that are merely combustible under ordinary conditions can become explosive when dispersed, confined, or suddenly released.

Chemically, an explosion is driven by a large exothermic change and a large positive entropy change, and the gaseous products, such as carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen, contain strong bonds of nearly 1 MJ/mole. Most commercial explosives are organic compounds containing –NO₂, –ONO₂, or –NHNO₂ groups, including nitroglycerin, TNT, HMX, PETN, and nitrocellulose.

Early thermal weapons such as [[Greek fire]] existed in ancient times. Taoist alchemists in China, searching for an elixir of eternal life, created the earliest gunpowder from coal, saltpeter, and sulfur, and it first saw use in warfare in 1161. Nitroglycerin, developed in 1847, was the first explosive stronger than black powder to see widespread use. Because it is liquid and unstable, it was replaced by nitrocellulose and trinitrotoluene in 1863, and by smokeless powder and [[Dynamite|dynamite]] in 1867. Dynamite was invented by Alfred Nobel in 1867, who stabilized nitroglycerin. World War I saw the adoption of TNT in artillery shells. Modern weapons largely use more powerful explosives such as C-4 and PETN.

The largest commercial application is [[Mining|mining]], which favors nitrate-based explosives such as mixtures of [[Ammonium nitrate|ammonium nitrate]] and fuel oil (ANFO). Explosives are also used in explosion welding, which cladds carbon steel or aluminium plate with a harder or more corrosion-resistant layer.
